video_title: Matthew Mezinskis: This Model Says Bitcoin Hits $1.1M In 2033
gist: Bitcoin power-law researcher Matthew Mezinskis explains that his log-log regression model currently puts fair value near $145K (versus a spot price that dipped to the 1st-2nd percentile of historical valuation before bouncing from the low-$60Ks to high-$70Ks/$80K), projects roughly $1.1M by 2033-2034 on trend, and argues Bitcoin's decelerating ~40%-to-20% CAGR power curve must eventually converge with traditional exponential (debt-compatible) growth rather than break to the downside.

themes.theme: Power Law Model Mechanics & Current Valuation

insights.claim: Matthew Mezinskis' Bitcoin power-law regression currently puts trend/fair value at roughly $145,000 while spot price was trading around half that (roughly $70-80K, having bounced off a low-$60Ks base), implying Bitcoin is deeply undervalued relative to its long-run log-log trend.
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: A large trend-value gap is the model's core buy signal; watchers of this framework would treat the current spot-to-trend discount as a statistically favorable accumulation zone.

insights.claim: Under Mezinskis' power-law model, Bitcoin's price is expected to double for every 13% increase in Bitcoin's total age (in days) — a mathematical doubling rule distinct from any fixed time period.
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: Gives investors a reusable, age-based (not calendar-based) framework for estimating how long future doublings should take as Bitcoin matures and growth decelerates.
insights.quote: For every 13% increase in the life of Bitcoin, the price doubles.

insights.claim: By the same power-law doubling logic, a 10x move requires roughly 50% of Bitcoin's current age to elapse; since Bitcoin is about 17 years old, that points to roughly an 8-year horizon (around 2033-2034) for the trend line to reach approximately $1.1 million per Bitcoin.
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: Gives a headline long-horizon price target ($1.1M by 2033-34) investors can track the model against, while explicitly being trend value, not a guaranteed spot price.
insights.quote: What about 10x? How do we 10x the price? The answer there is 50%.

insights.claim: Projecting the power curve out roughly 8 years from the 2026 recording date puts the trend value at about $1.1 million per Bitcoin around 2033-2034.
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: This is the specific, quotable price target the episode title references; investors should treat it as a trend-line projection, not a floor or ceiling.
insights.quote: lo and behold 1.1 million per bitcoin on the power curve

insights.claim: At the point Mezinskis was updating the model (mid-2026, ~6,400 days into Bitcoin's life, trend value ~$140K), the next doubling requires about 825 days (roughly 2.3 years), consistent with the 13%-of-age rule.
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete near-term checkpoint (a doubling window into roughly late 2028) to test the model's forecasting accuracy against.

insights.claim: During the summer 2026 drawdown, Bitcoin's price sat at roughly the 1st-2nd percentile of its historical power-law valuation distribution, meaning about 98% of past observations were relatively more expensive versus trend than the price was at that point.
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: An extreme percentile reading is the model's clearest statistical 'cheap' signal and, per the guest, was followed by a sharp bounce from the low-$60Ks to the high-$70Ks/$80K.
insights.quote: it's 98% more likely that the price should be higher than it was

insights.claim: The power-law curve statistically fits Bitcoin's full price history far better than a naive exponential trend: roughly 96% R-squared for the power fit versus roughly 85% R-squared for an exponential fit.
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: Quantifies why the guest prefers the power-law framework over simpler exponential extrapolations that many retail 'YouTube thumbnail' forecasts implicitly use.
insights.quote: about 85% R squar for exponential, 96% for power.

insights.claim: As an out-of-sample robustness test, fitting the power law using only data through September 2016 and extrapolating forward would have projected a trend value of about $200,000 today, versus the actual (all-data) trend value of $145,000 — a $50,000 miss after roughly a decade, which Mezinskis frames as evidence the model is structurally resilient.
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: A ten-year-old model missing by only ~$50K on a ~$145K trend value is a meaningful backtest in the model's favor versus rival models that have missed by orders of magnitude.

themes.theme: Power Law vs. Rival Forecasting Models

insights.claim: Plan B's original 2019 stock-to-flow model would imply a Bitcoin price of roughly $824,000 today, versus an actual price in the $70,000 range — an order-of-magnitude overshoot.
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence for investors to discount stock-to-flow-based long-term price targets that still circulate in Bitcoin discourse.

insights.claim: Plan B's revised 2020 stock-to-flow model (which added gold and silver as variables) implies a Bitcoin price of roughly $6.6 million today — an even larger miss than the original 2019 model, showing that adding variables made the model less accurate, not more.
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: Illustrates a general modeling lesson (added complexity/variables can degrade rather than improve out-of-sample accuracy) relevant to evaluating any crypto valuation model.

insights.claim: The structural flaw in stock-to-flow models, per Mezinskis, is that they are not 'scale invariant' — they cannot correctly project how Bitcoin's future stock-to-flow ratio will evolve, so their price projections systematically diverge from reality as time passes.
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: Gives investors a specific technical reason (not just 'it was wrong') to distrust stock-to-flow-style forecasts going forward, versus regression-based power-law models that are scale invariant.

insights.claim: If Bitcoin's price history were instead fit to a simple exponential trend (the type of trend that fits gold and stocks), the naive extrapolation would imply an absurd ~$18 million Bitcoin price by 2033 — used explicitly to debunk simplistic exponential-growth price predictions.
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: A useful benchmark for investors to sanity-check any 'Bitcoin grows exponentially forever' price target they encounter online.

insights.claim: Mezinskis and researcher Giovanni Santostasi (referred to as 'Giovanni' and associated with a 'Bitcoin science institute') independently arrived at Bitcoin's power-law relationship around the same time in 2018, with Santostasi publishing a few months before Mezinskis; both continue researching the framework alongside other analysts such as Steven Perrino ('Steven Parano' in the transcript).
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: Establishes provenance/credibility of the power-law approach as a multi-researcher, independently-replicated finding rather than a single analyst's proprietary chart.

themes.theme: Four-Year Cycle: Still Intact But Muted

insights.claim: Mezinskis maintains the classic Bitcoin four-year halving cycle remains fully intact despite widespread claims that it has 'broken' — price extended above trend roughly a year and a half after the halving, then rolled over about a year after that, matching the pattern of prior cycles.
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: Directly contradicts the popular 2024-25 narrative that the four-year cycle is dead; if he's right, cycle-timing frameworks (buy near halving lows, expect a top ~18 months post-halving) remain usable.

insights.claim: Unlike the 2013, 2017, and 2021 cycle tops, which blew well past the power law's 80th percentile valuation band, the 2024-2025 cycle only briefly touched roughly the 70th-80th percentile before rolling over — the first cycle with no true blow-off top.
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: A muted top with no euphoric blow-off is, per the guest, evidence against needing an equally violent 70-80% drawdown this cycle.

insights.claim: The subdued 2024-2025 cycle top is attributed to spot Bitcoin ETF approval (January 2024) plus political catalysts (Trump's election, Cynthia Lummis's strategic-reserve legislation talk) pulling institutional buying and price appreciation forward in time, effectively 'front-running' the power-law trend rather than producing a late-cycle euphoric spike.
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: Suggests future cycles could be structurally different (smoother, less blow-off-prone) as more institutional capital enters via regulated wrappers ahead of retail mania.

insights.claim: The only prior cycle in which Bitcoin's price respected (stayed above) the power law's modeled lower probability bound during the bear was 2018; every other major drawdown — including the pandemic crash and the current 2025 decline — has pierced below that lower band before recovering, meaning statistically extreme downside prints are historically the norm rather than the exception.
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: Tempers expectations that price should stay inside modeled bands; investors using this framework should expect occasional band-piercing capitulation moves as normal, not a model failure.

insights.claim: Mezinskis weights a four-year miner-revenue-relative-to-market-cap model more heavily than Wall Street order flow as a cycle-position signal, while acknowledging ETF flows have an outsized (though so far bounded) short-term influence on where price sits relative to the power-law trend.
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: Points investors toward on-chain miner economics as a complementary signal to price-based valuation models, less distorted by short-term institutional flows.

insights.claim: Because the prior up-leg lacked a euphoric, parabolic blow-off, Mezinskis argues a 70-80% peak-to-trough correction in the current bear is statistically unlikely, barring a forced-liquidation event such as a hypothetical Michael Saylor/Strategy bankruptcy scenario, which he views as very low probability.
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: A tactical read that the recent ~$60K area is a probable-enough cycle low, useful for investors positioning around cycle-bottom timing.

insights.claim: Mezinskis says he was personally cautious/conservative through summer 2026, not expecting the rally from the low-$60Ks to the high-$70Ks/$80K that occurred while he was on holiday — an admission that his own framework under-called the timing of the most recent short-term move even while he remained structurally bullish on valuation.
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: A useful honesty check: even a rigorous quantitative framework doesn't reliably call short-term timing, only broad statistical valuation.

themes.theme: Bitcoin vs. Gold and the Global Fiat Monetary Base

insights.claim: Gold has grown at roughly a 5.7% CAGR over the last 55 years (doubling roughly every 12.5 years) on a straight exponential trend — a fundamentally different growth pattern than Bitcoin's decelerating power-law curve.
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: Reinforces that Bitcoin should not be modeled with the same trend math as gold, despite common 'digital gold' comparisons.

insights.claim: Gold recently made its sharpest upside move since 1980 and, per the guest's model, is sitting near the top of its 50-year exponential channel; despite this and the 'digital gold' narrative, Mezinskis does not expect a large capital rotation from gold into Bitcoin, expecting Bitcoin's independent power-trend growth to dominate instead.
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: Pushes back on a popular thesis (gold-to-Bitcoin rotation driving the next leg up) that many Bitcoin bulls rely on.

insights.claim: The combined global central-bank monetary base across roughly 100 currencies is about $26.2 trillion; the five largest are China (~$5.9T, largest), the US (~$5.4T), the Eurozone (~$4.8T), Japan (~$3.6-3.7T), and the UK (under $1T) — Bitcoin's market cap (~$1.35-1.5T) already exceeds the entire British pound monetary base.
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: Concrete milestone framing (bigger than GBP's base) for tracking Bitcoin's monetization progress against major fiat currencies.

insights.claim: Bitcoin's market cap as a share of total global fiat monetary base peaked at roughly 9% during the late-2025 rally and had retreated to roughly 5% by March, based on Mezinskis' slow-moving quarterly dominance index.
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: Gives a trackable macro-monetization metric distinct from price alone, useful for gauging Bitcoin's progress toward becoming a reserve-scale asset.

insights.claim: Extrapolating the global fiat monetary base's roughly 7-7.5% CAGR against Bitcoin's decelerating power-law market-cap growth curve, the two converge at roughly $80 trillion each in the late 2030s, which Mezinskis calls the point where 'fireworks' will likely happen in the relationship between Bitcoin and the fiat system.
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: Offers a long-horizon macro milestone (~$80T Bitcoin market cap, late 2030s) investors can use to frame multi-decade portfolio allocation rather than cycle-to-cycle trading.

insights.claim: Mezinskis argues that as tokenization of assets accelerates, the world will need one neutral base settlement asset, and that Bitcoin will ultimately absorb value from the broader crypto/tokenization space because it is 'the best asset still out there' with no real alternative.
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: Frames Bitcoin as the long-term beneficiary of the broader tokenization/on-chain-everything trend rather than a competitor being displaced by altchains.
insights.quote: everybody is going to be absorbed by Bitcoin because there's no other alternative to it.

themes.theme: The Grand Theory: Power Law vs. Exponential Endgame

insights.claim: Mezinskis' central long-run thesis is that if/when Bitcoin's power-law growth pattern eventually breaks, it will break upward toward constant exponential (Trad-Fi-style) growth rather than downward — because a break to the downside would contradict the mathematical resilience of the model he's tested.
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: Reframes the common fear ('what if the model breaks and price crashes') — per this framework, a break is more likely bullish (converging to steady compounding) than bearish.

insights.claim: Bitcoin's realized annualized growth rate is on an explicit decelerating schedule per the power law: roughly 2,000% in 2011, roughly 104% in 2017, just under 40% today, projected to fall to roughly 26-27% by the time Bitcoin reaches $1 million, and roughly 20% CAGR by around 2040.
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: Gives investors explicit expected-return decay milestones to compare against alternative assets (e.g., equities compounding near 20%/yr) when deciding portfolio weighting over time.

insights.claim: Mezinskis argues a structural reason Bitcoin must eventually shift from a power-law to an exponential growth pattern: an asset whose appreciation rate keeps mathematically declining cannot support debt/interest contracts against it, since lenders need a stable-or-rising expected return relative to their cost of capital — this is why he thinks Bitcoin will eventually be forced toward constant-CAGR behavior once it's integrated into leveraged Trad-Fi.
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: A non-obvious, largely unstated-elsewhere argument for why institutional adoption/leverage (credit against BTC, lending markets) could itself be the mechanism that forces Bitcoin off its power-law growth path.
insights.quote: you can't run a debt contract under a power law system.

insights.claim: Mezinskis frames two possible long-run endgames for Bitcoin: either (a) the entire financial system adopts Bitcoin's power-law-style growth pattern (a 'cypherpunk' outcome he views as impractical), or (b) Bitcoin itself converts to a constant exponential CAGR (echoing Michael Saylor's public framing) once fully absorbed into a leveraged, debt-based Trad-Fi system — and he considers outcome (b) the more likely path.
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: Sets up a testable long-run framework: watch for Bitcoin's growth-rate deceleration to flatten out into a constant rate as institutional debt/leverage products around it grow, as the tell that scenario (b) is playing out.

insights.claim: Mezinskis directly critiques Michael Saylor's public claim that Bitcoin will settle into a perpetual 21% CAGR, saying there is no mathematical justification for that specific figure beyond it echoing the 21 million BTC supply cap, calling it 'cheeky,' even though he thinks Saylor's broader intuition about Bitcoin eventually converging to a constant exponential growth rate could still prove directionally correct.
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: A useful nuance for investors who cite Saylor's 21%-forever framing as gospel — the number itself isn't derived from any model, only the directional convergence thesis is defensible.
insights.quote: there's no justification that Bitcoin would increase at 21% per year other than the fact that there's 21 million bitcoins and he's kind of appropriating the number 21

insights.claim: Mezinskis warns that if Bitcoin becomes fully financialized, leveraged, and KYC-controlled within the traditional financial/government system in order to reach very high valuations, that outcome represents a values trade-off — paraphrasing an idea (attributed by the guest to a conversation referenced by the host) that 'we're all rich, but that means the project failed' relative to Bitcoin's original cypherpunk sovereignty and censorship-resistance goals.
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: A reminder to price-focused investors that the most bullish price-integration scenario for Bitcoin could simultaneously represent a philosophical failure of its original decentralization/sovereignty value proposition.
insights.quote: we're all rich, but that means the project failed

insights.claim: The Netherlands had proposed a 36% unrealized capital-gains tax that would apply to Bitcoin and other assets; as of the recording, its implementation had just been postponed, and the host states he would relocate out of the Netherlands if it were ultimately enacted.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: A live, concrete jurisdictional tax-policy risk for European Bitcoin holders to monitor, with direct relocation implications if it passes.

insights.claim: Mezinskis argues that unrealized-gains taxation constitutes a form of regulatory capture that defeats self-custody as a protection: even holding Bitcoin in multi-signature wallets spread across multiple countries doesn't shield a holder from a home jurisdiction's tax claim on unrealized gains, since the tax doesn't depend on where custody sits.
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: Highlights a risk category (tax-based state capture) that no amount of self-custody or key-management sophistication can fully mitigate, distinct from theft/hacking risk.

insights.claim: Mezinskis frames aggressive unrealized-gains tax proposals as an early, concrete preview of the same 'capture' dynamic he describes in his long-run power-law-to-exponential thesis — i.e., the state/financial system pulling Bitcoin into its own rules rather than Bitcoin remaining outside them.
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: Links a near-term policy risk (unrealized gains tax) to the episode's broader long-run thesis about Bitcoin's eventual integration into (and potential capture by) the traditional financial/regulatory system.

themes.theme: Practical Application: Model as a Trading Framework

insights.claim: Mezinskis' explicit (self-described 'not financial advice') practical rule is to dollar-cost-average more aggressively when Bitcoin sits at extreme low percentiles of the power-law valuation distribution, and to trim/unload a portion of holdings when it sits at extreme high percentiles.
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: A concrete, rules-based contrarian rebalancing strategy investors could adapt using the guest's publicly available percentile/quantile charts.

insights.claim: Mezinskis admits he did not fully follow his own valuation discipline into the 2017 top — despite an earlier (pre-power-law) chart flagging overvaluation, he stayed overexposed, citing greed as the reason.
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: An honest behavioral-finance caveat: having a rigorous valuation framework doesn't guarantee an investor will act on it, especially near euphoric tops.

insights.claim: Mezinskis cites Peter Zeihan (transcribed as 'Peter Zion') telling Joe Rogan around the 2022 cycle low (when Bitcoin traded near $16,000) that Bitcoin was '$17,000 overvalued' — implying it should be worth close to zero — as an example of a prominent geopolitical/macro commentator opining on Bitcoin with no grounding in its actual price-trend mathematics.
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: A cautionary example for investors to weigh mainstream macro commentary on Bitcoin against quantitative trend evidence rather than pundit intuition.

insights.claim: Mezinskis says the influence of derivatives/leveraged 'paper Bitcoin' positioning on where price sits relative to the power-law trend is currently still fairly limited, though he separately acknowledges ETF flows have had an outsized (bounded) effect on pulling the 2024-25 cycle's price action forward.
insights.speaker: Matthew Mezinskis
insights.so_what: Suggests derivatives-driven distortion of the power-law signal is not yet a major confound for investors using the model, though this could change as leverage products grow.
